name: Breast ironing

lead: Breast ironing is a family practice in which a girl's budding breasts are repeatedly pressed, massaged or pounded, often with a heated object, with the aim of slowing or hiding their growth. Families who do it describe the goal as an appearance one: a flatter, less developed chest is believed to make a girl look younger and draw less sexual attention, protecting her from harassment, early pregnancy and early marriage.

It is best documented in Cameroon, where a 2006 survey reported that nearly one in four girls and women had experienced it, and it has been reported in several other West and Central African countries and among diaspora communities. Health researchers describe the practice as painful and harmful and as a form of gender-based violence, and campaigns by NGOs and international bodies aim to end it.

paras: Reports describe a female relative, most often the mother, applying pressure or massage to the girl's chest with objects such as a pestle, grinding stone, spatula, or leaves and coconut shells warmed over a fire, usually in private, sometimes over days to months. Some families use tight bands or cloths instead. It is a practice done to girls, usually between about 8 and 13, rather than a method adults choose for themselves. This article describes it for documentation only.

Researchers and clinicians report severe pain, burns, tissue damage, abscesses, infections, cysts, scarring and asymmetric breast development, along with fear, anxiety and body-image distress, and possible breastfeeding difficulties later in life. Reviews note that formal clinical studies are few. In the UK it is treated as child abuse, and the UN and national campaigns treat it as a human-rights concern.

angle.text: The practice is carried out with the stated goal of keeping a girl's chest flat so that she looks less developed. Whether it achieves that, or the protection families hope for, has not been shown, and reviews document injury and distress. It is done to girls by relatives, not chosen by them.

lead: Breast ironing, also called breast flattening, is a traditional practice in which the developing breasts of a pubescent girl are pounded, pressed or massaged, often with a heated object, in order to slow their growth or make them less noticeable. It is usually carried out by a close female relative such as a mother, grandmother or aunt [1][2]. The stated aim is about how a girl looks: with a flatter, less developed chest, families believe she will seem younger and attract less unwanted sexual attention [1][2].

It is most closely associated with Cameroon. A 2006 survey by the German agency GIZ of more than 5,000 girls and women reported that nearly one in four had undergone it, with much higher figures in some regions than in the Muslim north; similar practices have been reported in Nigeria, Togo, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya, Zimbabwe and elsewhere, and concern has been raised about diaspora communities in Britain [2]. Families who practise it describe it as protection against rape, early pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections and early marriage, and as a way to keep girls in school [2][3].

Researchers and international bodies describe it as harmful and as a form of gender-based violence, and have called for more research, since reviews note limited clinical data [3][4][5]. It appears on this wiki because it is a practice aimed at deliberately changing breast appearance, and is documented here with its reported harms.

paras: In breast ironing, pressure, massage or pounding is applied to a girl's chest when the first signs of breast growth appear. Tools reported in surveys and reviews include wooden pestles, grinding stones, spatulas, ladles, hammers, coconut shells and leaves, frequently warmed over coals or a fire; some families use elastic belts or tight cloths to bind the chest instead [1][2]. It is usually done in a private place such as a kitchen, often early morning or at dusk, partly to keep it from fathers and other men [2].

Duration is reported as anything from about a week to several months, with sessions repeated daily or more [1][2]. Because the procedure is performed on children by relatives, accounts stress that it is typically a family decision, not the girl's [3][4].

Writers suggest the practice may derive from older forms of breast massage used to even out breast size or ease nursing pain [2]. Reviews tie its current form to concerns about girls' safety: parents see visible breast development as a signal of sexual maturity and fear harassment, rape and early pregnancy, and some cite earlier puberty and changing marriage patterns [2][3]. Mothers who perform it often describe it as an act of protection [3].
A 2006 survey found that 39% of Cameroonian women opposed the practice, 41% supported it and 26% were indifferent [2].

Reviews describe severe pain, burns, tissue damage, infections and abscesses, cysts, scarring and asymmetric or damaged breast tissue, with possible later breastfeeding difficulties; psychological effects such as fear, anxiety and body-image distress are also described [1][3][4]. A narrative review frames it through human rights and transcultural nursing and lists mammary-gland damage and long-term complications among its consequences [3]. Authors of a 2021 global-health overview describe it as under-reported and under-studied [4].

Researchers have said that rigorous clinical data are scarce; a scoping-review protocol published in 2026 aims to map prevalence, motivations, health and social impacts, and interventions in Africa [6].

The UN has counted breast ironing among forms of harmful practices against women and girls, and from 2006 GIZ and the Cameroonian network RENATA (Network of Aunties) ran awareness campaigns supported by Cameroon's women's ministry [2]. Reuters reported in 2014 that campaigns had halved the rate, though the figure is attributed to campaigners [2]. In the UK the practice is treated as child abuse, and the charity CAME Women and Girls Development Organisation has worked with the Metropolitan Police on awareness [2]. Coverage has included the BBC (2006 and 2019), CNN (2011), The Independent (2013) and The Guardian (2019) [2]. The BMJ and Archives of Disease in Childhood have published pieces calling it an under-recognised form of gender-based violence [7][8].

No controlled clinical studies of breast ironing as an intervention exist. Research consists of surveys, narrative and scoping reviews, and clinical commentaries describing prevalence and harms [3][4][6][7][8]. A 2024 narrative review reports physical, psychological and social consequences, and a 2026 scoping review of the topic argues it is under-represented in gender-based-violence scholarship and clinical practice [3][9].

timeline.event: The UN identifies breast ironing among overlooked forms of discrimination against women and girls [2].
Cameroonian researchers document the practice across all ten regions of the country [1].
GIZ survey reports nearly one in four girls and women in Cameroon affected; GIZ and RENATA launch campaigns [2].
BMJ and Guardian coverage draws attention to UK cases [2][7].
Journal of Global Health publishes an overview describing the practice as under-reported [4].
